To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

AM fungi secrete symbiotic signalling molecules that are a mixture sulphated and non sulphated lipochitooligo-saccharides (sLCOs and nLCOs) that induce root growth and branching in legumes by the symbiotic signalling pathway.

Glomus fungi produce a mixture of sulphate and non-sulphotated lipochitooligiosaccharides (sulphated and non-sulfated LCOs) that stimulate AM in plants from three different families (Fabaceae: Medicago truncatulua; Asteraceae: Solanum lycopersicon; Umbellifera: Petroselinum crispum).
Glomus sp. produces diffusible symbiosis signals that are sulphated and non sulphated simple lipochito-oligosaccharides that stimulate AM in plant species belonging to different families.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of plant-fungal interactions and how they are regulated.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the symbiotic association between plant roots and arbuscular mycorehizal fungi (AMF), which is the most widespread symbiosis on land.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms involved in symbiotic interactions between plants and fungi.
